hops.title: The hemoglobin crystals that fell apart in air
hops.text: In 1938, Felix Haurowitz put crystals of oxygen-free hemoglobin under a microscope and let air creep in under the cover slip. As oxygen reached them, the purple, six-sided crystals dissolved, and bright red crystals of a different shape grew in their place. A crystal is molecules packed in a regular pattern, and oxygen had swapped one pattern for another. Haurowitz took it as a sign that the whole molecule changes shape when it binds oxygen. Nobody could see a protein's atoms yet. His distant relative Max Perutz later spent decades on hemoglobin with X-rays and finally showed both shapes side by side.

sources.citation: Brunori, M. (2024). Wandering about allostery. Biology Direct, 19, 64 (describing Haurowitz, F., 1938, Hoppe-Seyler's Z. Physiol. Chem. 254:266-274).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A vintage brass microscope on a wooden bench, with a magnified view of purple crystal plates dissolving while bright red crystals grow.
image.caption: In 1938, purple oxygen-free hemoglobin crystals dissolved in air and red ones grew: a clue that oxygen reshapes the protein.

hops.title: How crocodile hemoglobin lets go of oxygen on a long dive
hops.text: Crocodiles can stay underwater for more than an hour, and their hemoglobin has a regulator ours does not use. Our red cells tune hemoglobin with 2,3-BPG. Crocodile hemoglobin answers to bicarbonate, the form most carbon dioxide takes in blood. While a crocodile holds its breath, bicarbonate builds up, binds where the subunits meet, lowers hemoglobin's oxygen affinity and releases oxygen to the tissues. In 1995, a team moved that switch into human hemoglobin with just 12 amino-acid changes, even though the two proteins differ at about a third of the α chain and half of the β chain.

sources.citation: Komiyama, N. H., Miyazaki, G., Tame, J., & Nagai, K. (1995). Transplanting a unique allosteric effect from crocodile into human haemoglobin. Nature, 373, 244-246.
Natarajan, C., et al. (2023). Evolution and molecular basis of a novel allosteric property of crocodilian hemoglobin. Current Biology, 33, 98-108 (the 12 substitutions).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A crocodile resting under clear green river water with small bubbles rising toward the sunlit surface.
image.caption: Bicarbonate that builds up during a long dive tells crocodile hemoglobin to let go of its oxygen.

hops.afterHeading: When the shapes betray you: hemoglobin pathology
hops.title: The colors of beef in the meat case
hops.text: Next time you pass a supermarket meat case, compare a vacuum-sealed package of beef with an ordinary clear-wrapped tray. The sealed beef is usually darker and purplish: shut away from air, its myoglobin carries no oxygen. Under wrap that lets air through, fresh beef usually looks bright red, because oxygen binds myoglobin's heme iron. Once that iron is oxidized to Fe³⁺, meat turns brown. Carbon monoxide grips myoglobin's heme much as it grips hemoglobin's, and holds it a stable red. United States rules let packers fill some sealed packages with 0.4% carbon monoxide; the European Union bans it, partly over concern that the lasting color could hide the meat's age.

sources.citation: Djenane, D., & Roncalés, P. (2018). Carbon monoxide in meat and fish packaging: advantages and limits. Foods, 7(2), 12.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Two packages of raw beef in a store case: a vacuum-sealed purplish piece beside a bright red tray under clear wrap.
image.caption: Sealed away from air, myoglobin leaves beef purplish; oxygen on its heme iron turns it bright red.
